questions.question: What is cloud-native and why does it exist? It is a set of practices for building applications that exploit cloud elasticity and resilience — so they scale, heal, and deploy independently.
questions.title: Cloud-Native Fundamentals
questions.direct_answer: Cloud-native is an approach to building and running applications that exploits the cloud's elasticity, distributed nature, and managed services — containers, microservices, declarative config, and observability — rather than lifting a fixed-size server app onto a VM. It exists because apps designed for a single long-lived server fail in the cloud: they can't scale per component, can't heal on failure, and can't deploy without downtime, while cloud-native apps scale horizontally, self-heal, and ship continuously.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand cloud-native as a set of design principles (12-Factor, stateless, disposable, observable) not just 'runs on a cloud', and can name what each principle buys you.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Equating cloud-native with 'uses Kubernetes' — the platform is a means; the principles (statelessness, disposability, externalized config) are what actually make an app cloud-native.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the 12-Factor principles and what each buys — config externalized so the same build runs anywhere, disposability so instances can be killed and replaced, logs as streams so the platform owns aggregation — and note that cloud-native is design, Kubernetes is one runtime for it.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Cloud-native is a way of building and running applications that exploit the cloud's elasticity and resilience — containers, microservices, declarative configuration, and observability — rather than treating the cloud as a remote data center of fixed VMs. It exists because apps designed for a single long-lived server can't scale per component, can't survive instance loss, and can't deploy without downtime, which wastes the cloud's core advantages. The 12-Factor App methodology is the canonical checklist of design principles that make a Java service behave well in this model.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas: (1) the 12-Factor principles — config in the environment (not code), backing services as attached resources, logs as event streams, disposability — encode the design rules; (2) statelessness — instances hold no session state, so any can be killed/replaced/scaled; (3) disposability — fast startup and graceful shutdown let the platform recycle instances safely; (4) externalized config — the same immutable build artifact runs in dev/staging/prod via different env config; (5) observability — metrics/logs/traces are emitted for an external platform to aggregate, not stored locally; (6) declarative over imperative — describe desired state, let the platform reconcile it.

sections.title: 12-Factor config and disposability in a Spring Boot service
Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension is flexibility versus operational cost: cloud-native design buys elasticity, independent scaling, and resilience but demands you externalize config, build observability, and operate distributed systems — none of which a monolith-on-a-VM needs. A second tension: statelessness is required for safe horizontal scaling, but some real problems are stateful (caches, sessions, workflows), which must then be moved to a backing service (Redis, Kafka) — the state doesn't disappear, it moves. The third: the same build-artifact-anywhere principle (Factor III) is powerful but requires discipline around config and secrets to be real.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Cloud-native is design for the cloud's elasticity and resilience, not just 'runs on a cloud' — containers and K8s are means, not the definition.
The 12-Factor principles are the canonical checklist: config in env, backing services as URLs, stateless disposable processes, logs as streams.
Statelessness lets the platform kill, replace, or scale any instance at any time — state moves to a backing service, it doesn't disappear.
The same immutable build artifact runs in any environment; only environment config (and secrets) differ — no rebuilds per env.
Observability (metrics/logs/traces) is emitted for the platform to aggregate; apps never own log files, which die with the instance.
Disposability — fast startup and graceful shutdown on SIGTERM — is what lets a platform recycle instances without dropping in-flight requests.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Cloud-native is a way of building apps that actually exploits what the cloud offers — elasticity, resilience, managed services — instead of just running an old server app on a VM. It exists because apps designed for one long-lived server can't scale per component or survive instance loss, which wastes the cloud entirely. The checklist I anchor on is 12-Factor: config lives in the environment, not the jar; backing services are attached by URL; processes are stateless and disposable so the platform can kill or scale any instance anytime; logs go out as streams that the platform aggregates, never to local files. The part people miss is that cloud-native is design — statelessness, disposability, externalized config — and Kubernetes is just one runtime that runs that design. The state doesn't disappear either; if your problem is stateful, you move it to a backing service like Redis or Kafka.

followup_questions: Why must a cloud-native process be stateless, and where does its state go instead?
How does Factor III (config in the environment) let the same jar run in dev, staging, and prod?
What does 'disposability' require of a Spring Boot service on SIGTERM, and what breaks if you ignore it?
Why are logs emitted as streams rather than written to local files in a cloud-native app?
How does moving to containers change the blast radius of an instance failure compared to a monolith on a VM?

questions.question: Explain the 12-Factor App methodology and how it maps to modern cloud-native Java services.
questions.title: 12-Factor App: Principles and Modern Cloud-Native Application
questions.direct_answer: The **12-Factor App** is a methodology codified by Heroku for building SaaS applications that are easy to deploy, scale, and operate in the cloud. The twelve factors are: **(I) Codebase** (one repo, many deploys), **(II) Dependencies** (explicit, isolated), **(III) Config** (in environment), **(IV) Backing services** (treated as attached resources), **(V) Build, release, run** (strict separation), **(VI) Processes** (stateless, share-nothing), **(VII) Port binding** (self-contained, exports via port), **(VIII) Concurrency** (scale horizontally via process model), **(IX) Disposability** (fast startup, graceful shutdown), **(X) Dev/prod parity** (keep environments similar), **(XI) Logs** (event stream to stdout), **(XII) Admin processes** (one-off commands as identical processes). For Java/Spring Boot: externalize config with `@ConfigurationProperties` + env vars, package as fat JARs or containers, emit logs to stdout (not files), use Kubernetes for process management and scaling, Flyway/Liquibase for schema. Modern additions (Beyond the 12): API versioning, telemetry/observability, authentication as service, multi-tenant awareness.

interviewer_intent.testing: Cloud-native fundamentals, ability to map principles to real code/infra
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reciting factors without showing how they map to actual Spring/K8s practices
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss 'Beyond 12 Factors', trade-offs (e.g., stateless vs performance caching), CNCF patterns

sections.title: Why 12-Factor Exists
sections.content:
In 2011 Heroku engineers codified patterns they saw in reliably-deployable SaaS apps. The goal: apps that can be **built once and deployed anywhere**, **scaled horizontally** without architectural rework, and **managed by simple orchestration** (process-per-concern).

It predates Kubernetes but reads like a design spec *for* Kubernetes. It's opinionated, language-agnostic, and pragmatic. Most modern cloud-native practices — containers, 12-factor is baked in — stateless services, env-based config, structured logging, graceful shutdown — trace back to these principles.

**When to use it:** default for new web services, SaaS, microservices in cloud. Not all 12 factors apply equally to *every* system (databases themselves aren't 12-factor apps; they're backing services), but the principles guide design and ops.

sections.title: The 12 Factors — What They Mean and How Java/Spring Boot Applies
sections.content:
**I. Codebase** — one repo per app; many deploys (dev, staging, prod) from same codebase.
- *Java/Spring*: Git repo; use tags/branches for environments, not separate repos.

**II. Dependencies** — declare all deps explicitly; never rely on system packages.
- *Java/Spring*: Maven/Gradle with pinned versions; fat-jar packaging; distroless/JDK base images in Docker.

**III. Config** — config that differs between deploys lives in the environment (env vars), not code or tracked files.
- *Java/Spring*: `application.yml` for defaults; `@ConfigurationProperties` pulls overrides from `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` etc.; never check secrets into Git.

**IV. Backing services** — DBs, queues, caches are attached resources, swappable via config.
- *Java/Spring*: DataSource URL points to dev Postgres locally or RDS in prod; Kafka bootstrap servers from env.

**V. Build, release, run** — strict separation.
- *Build*: compile, run tests, package (create container image)
- *Release*: combine build artifact + environment config = versioned release
- *Run*: execute the release
- *Java/Spring*: CI builds `:1.2.3` image; CD promotes image + env config to staging/prod; rollback = deploy previous image.

**VI. Processes** — app executes as one or more **stateless, share-nothing** processes; any state goes to backing services.
- *Java/Spring*: no file-on-disk state, no session-in-memory state (use Spring Session + Redis if needed).

**VII. Port binding** — app is self-contained; exports HTTP (or other protocol) by binding to a port; no reliance on an external webserver.
- *Java/Spring*: embedded Tomcat/Netty; `server.port` from env.

**VIII. Concurrency** — scale by running more processes (horizontal); processes are atomic scale units.
- *Java/Spring*: K8s Deployment replicas; HPA based on CPU / custom metrics. Don't try to scale vertically forever.

**IX. Disposability** — fast startup (seconds), graceful shutdown (flush in-flight work, close DB pools on SIGTERM).
- *Java/Spring*: `server.shutdown=graceful` + `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s`; K8s `preStop` hook + `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`.

**X. Dev/prod parity** — keep dev, staging, prod as similar as possible: same DB engine, same queue, short time gap between commit and deploy.
- *Java/Spring*: Testcontainers spins up real Postgres/Kafka in tests; avoid H2 in-memory for integration.

**XI. Logs** — treat logs as event streams; write to stdout; aggregation is infra's job.
- *Java/Spring*: Logback to stdout in JSON; Fluent Bit / Datadog agent ships to log store.

**XII. Admin processes** — run one-off admin tasks (migrations, backfills) as identical processes against the release.
- *Java/Spring*: Flyway runs on startup for migrations; backfills as K8s Jobs using same image + different command.

sections.title: Beyond 12 Factors — Kevin Hoffman's Additions and 2020s Practices
sections.content:
Kevin Hoffman (Pivotal) wrote 'Beyond the Twelve Factor App' with practical additions:

- **API first**: design the API contract before implementation. Enables parallel team work and easier client evolution.
- **Telemetry**: embrace observability from day one. Metrics, distributed traces, structured logs. Otherwise you can't debug scale.
- **Authentication and Authorization**: no app is truly 'open'; treat authn/authz as a cross-cutting concern early. OAuth2/OIDC, JWTs, service mesh mTLS.

Modern additions I'd add for 2020s cloud-native:

- **Security by default**: secrets from vault/sealed-secrets; image scanning; SBOM; non-root container users; read-only rootfs.
- **Multi-tenant awareness**: if your service will serve >1 tenant, bake it into the data model and observability from day one (hard to retrofit).
- **Idempotency**: HTTP endpoints accept idempotency keys; message consumers handle duplicate delivery. Essential for retries and exactly-once semantics.
- **Progressive delivery**: feature flags, canaries, blue/green. Reduces deploy risk.
- **Cost awareness**: resource requests/limits, autoscaling policies, ephemeral environments that tear down. Cloud bill bites hard without discipline.
- **Graceful degradation**: circuit breakers, fallbacks, serving cached data when backend is down. 12-factor says nothing about this but it matters in distributed systems.

**Where 12-factor strains:**

1. **Stateful services** (databases, message brokers) inherently violate 'stateless processes'. 12-factor applies to the *application*, not the backing services.
2. **In-memory caches** for performance (e.g., reference data) violate strict statelessness. Pragmatic compromise: keep caches recoverable from backing store.
3. **Long-running jobs** (hours-long batch): disposability is hard. Checkpointing + idempotent processing helps.
4. **Very stateful workflows** (sagas, user sessions): use backing service for state; keep process truly stateless. Spring Session, Redis, etc.
5. **WebSocket servers** with connection state: either keep state external (ideal) or accept sticky connections as necessary trade-off.

sections.title: Putting It Together: A 12-Factor Spring Boot Service
sections.content:
**Repo structure (Factor I):**
```
acme-orders/
├── src/
├── Dockerfile
├── helm/           # K8s manifests
├── pom.xml
└── .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

**Dependencies (II):** Maven; production image:
```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-jammy
COPY target/app.jar /app.jar
USER 1000
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"]
```

**Config (III) + Backing services (IV):**
```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: ${DB_URL}
    username: ${DB_USER}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: ${KAFKA_BROKERS}
```
Secrets from Vault / Sealed Secrets / CSI driver, not plain env.

**Build/Release/Run (V):**
- CI: build image `acme-orders:1.2.3`, push to registry
- CD: Argo CD deploys `acme-orders:1.2.3` to cluster
- Release = image + ConfigMap/Secret snapshot

**Processes (VI):** `@RestController` classes; no files written to disk; sessions in Spring Session + Redis; S3 for blob storage.

**Port binding (VII):**
```yaml
server:
  port: ${PORT:8080}
  shutdown: graceful
```

**Concurrency (VIII):**
```yaml
# deployment.yaml
spec:
  replicas: 3
---
# hpa.yaml
spec:
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
```

**Disposability (IX):**
```yaml
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s
```
K8s:
```yaml
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec:
      command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 10"]   # allow LB to drain
```

**Dev/prod parity (X):** Testcontainers spins up real Postgres in integration tests; same image from CI runs on local k3s and prod cluster.

**Logs (XI):**
```yaml
logging:
  pattern:
    console: '{"ts":"%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS}","level":"%level","logger":"%logger","msg":"%msg","trace":"%X{traceId:-}","span":"%X{spanId:-}"}%n'
```
Kubernetes picks up container stdout; Fluent Bit ships to Elasticsearch/Datadog.

**Admin processes (XII):**
- Flyway on startup for migrations (idempotent)
- One-off K8s Job using same image to backfill data:
```yaml
kind: Job
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: backfill
          image: acme-orders:1.2.3
          command: ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar", "--spring.profiles.active=backfill", "--spring.main.web-application-type=none"]
```

sections.title: Trade-offs and When to Deviate
sections.content:
**Why 12-Factor wins for most services:**
- Portability: any k8s or PaaS runs it
- Scalability: horizontal scaling is built-in
- Maintainability: clear separation of config, build, release
- Observability: stdout logs + env config make debugging consistent

**Costs / where it gets hard:**
- **Config in env is rough for lots of config**: a service with 50 env vars becomes a pain. Use ConfigMaps + Secrets (still env-mountable but version-controlled).
- **Secrets in env are visible to anyone with pod access**: use Vault, CSI drivers, or at least K8s Secrets with RBAC.
- **Strict statelessness hurts caches**: reading a reference table every request is wasteful. Pragmatic compromise: in-memory cache that's refreshable from DB, treated as disposable (if lost, recomputes).
- **Fast startup fights with Java's bootstrap cost**: 30-second startup violates 'fast'. Solutions: AOT compile (Spring Native), SnapStart (AWS Lambda), smaller classpaths.
- **Log-to-stdout with large volumes**: high-throughput services may overrun stdout pipes; sample or rate-limit logs.

**Common anti-patterns to avoid:**
1. **Config checked into code**: 'it's just dev config' — until dev and prod diverge silently
2. **Separate repos per env**: makes 'one codebase, many deploys' impossible
3. **File-based logs that a sidecar tails**: works, but stdout-to-container-runtime is the k8s-native path; simpler
4. **Session state in JVM memory**: breaks on pod termination; use Spring Session + Redis
5. **DB migrations outside release process**: 'run this SQL by hand' is fragile; use Flyway
6. **Long sync startup (JPA warmup, cache loads)**: makes rolling deploys sluggish; lazy-init and warm asynchronously
7. **No health checks or probes that return 'healthy' without checking DB connectivity**: leads to traffic to unhealthy pods

**When to deviate:**
- **Data services** (databases, search engines): inherently stateful; use StatefulSets, PVCs, careful backup strategy
- **ML inference services with large models**: may need model preload on GPU; startup may be longer; use readiness probe to gate traffic
- **Legacy applications**: full 12-factor migration is a project; incrementalize by factor (logs first is usually easiest)
- **Monoliths being modernized**: not every factor applies; start with externalizing config and logs

**Strategic take:**

12-Factor is a **floor, not a ceiling**. Following it doesn't make you cloud-native; it makes you *deployable*. Modern cloud-native adds observability, resilience patterns, security posture, FinOps, and progressive delivery on top. Start with 12-factor as the bare minimum for anything new, then layer on what you need.

The biggest practical benefit: **onboarding speed**. A new service that follows 12-factor is understandable in 30 minutes; deploy pipeline is boilerplate. Deviating for 'good reasons' is fine; deviating *without knowing* is how teams end up with snowflake services.

**Interview angle:** most interviewers don't expect you to recite all 12 — they want to know you can connect principles to real code/infra. Name a factor, explain what it means, give a Java/K8s example, note where it strains.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **12 factors** from Heroku (2011): codebase, deps, config, services, build/release/run, processes, port, concurrency, disposability, dev/prod parity, logs, admin
- **Java/Spring Boot**: `@ConfigurationProperties` + env vars; embedded server; stdout logs; Flyway on startup; K8s for scale
- **Factor VI (stateless)** is the keystone — enables horizontal scaling
- **Factor IX (disposability)**: fast start + graceful shutdown; K8s SIGTERM + preStop hook
- **Factor XI (logs)**: write to stdout, let infra aggregate (Fluent Bit, Datadog)
- **Beyond 12**: API-first, telemetry, authn/authz, security, multi-tenancy, idempotency
- **Stateful services** (DB, MQ) are backing services, not 12-factor apps
- **Common anti-patterns**: config in code, per-env repos, JVM-memory sessions, no health checks
- **Strategic role**: 12-factor is floor not ceiling; modern adds observability, resilience, FinOps, progressive delivery

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The 12-Factor App is a methodology codified by Heroku in 2011 for building SaaS applications that are easy to deploy, scale, and operate in the cloud.

**The twelve factors**
1. Codebase - one repo, many deploys
2. Dependencies - explicit, isolated
3. Config - in environment
4. Backing services - attached resources
5. Build, release, run - strict separation
6. Processes - stateless, share-nothing
7. Port binding - self-contained, exports via port
8. Concurrency - scale horizontally via process model
9. Disposability - fast startup, graceful shutdown
10. Dev/prod parity - keep environments similar
11. Logs - event stream to stdout
12. Admin processes - one-off commands as identical processes

**Why 12-Factor exists**
- Heroku engineers codified patterns from reliably-deployable SaaS apps
- Goal: apps built once, deployed anywhere, scaled horizontally, managed by simple orchestration
- Predates Kubernetes but reads like a design spec for it
- Modern cloud-native traces back to these principles

**Each factor with Java/Spring application**

*I. Codebase*
- One repo per app; many deploys from same codebase
- Git repo; tags/branches for environments, not separate repos

*II. Dependencies*
- Declare all deps explicitly; never system packages
- Maven/Gradle pinned versions; fat-jar packaging; distroless/JDK base images

*III. Config*
- Config differing between deploys in environment (env vars)
- application.yml for defaults; @ConfigurationProperties pulls SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL etc.
- Never check secrets into Git

*IV. Backing services*
- DBs, queues, caches as attached resources, swappable via config
- DataSource URL = dev Postgres locally or RDS in prod; Kafka brokers from env

*V. Build, release, run*
- Build: compile, test, package (container image)
- Release: artifact + env config = versioned release
- Run: execute release
- CI builds :1.2.3 image; CD promotes to staging/prod; rollback = prev image

*VI. Processes*
- Stateless, share-nothing; state goes to backing services
- No file-on-disk state; no session-in-memory (use Spring Session + Redis)

*VII. Port binding*
- Self-contained; exports HTTP by binding to port; no external webserver
- Embedded Tomcat/Netty; server.port from env

*VIII. Concurrency*
- Scale by more processes (horizontal); atomic scale units
- K8s Deployment replicas; HPA on CPU / custom metrics

*IX. Disposability*
- Fast startup (seconds), graceful shutdown (flush, close pools on SIGTERM)
- server.shutdown=graceful + timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s
- K8s preStop hook + terminationGracePeriodSeconds

*X. Dev/prod parity*
- Same DB engine, same queue; short commit-to-deploy gap
- Testcontainers spins real Postgres/Kafka in tests; avoid H2

*XI. Logs*
- Event streams to stdout; aggregation = infra's job
- Logback JSON to stdout; Fluent Bit/Datadog ships to log store

*XII. Admin processes*
- One-off admin tasks (migrations, backfills) as identical processes against release
- Flyway on startup; K8s Jobs using same image + different command

**Beyond 12 Factors - Kevin Hoffman + modern**

*Hoffman's additions*
- API first: design contract before implementation
- Telemetry: metrics, traces, structured logs from day one
- Authn/authz: cross-cutting concern early; OAuth2/OIDC, mTLS

*Modern 2020s additions*
- Security by default: vault secrets, image scanning, SBOM, non-root containers, read-only rootfs
- Multi-tenant awareness: bake into data model + observability from day one
- Idempotency: HTTP idempotency keys, consumer dedup; essential for retries
- Progressive delivery: feature flags, canaries, blue/green
- Cost awareness: resource limits, autoscaling, ephemeral environments
- Graceful degradation: circuit breakers, fallbacks, cached data

**Where 12-Factor strains**
1. Stateful services (DBs, brokers) inherently violate 'stateless processes'
2. In-memory caches for performance violate strict statelessness
3. Long-running jobs (hours): disposability hard; use checkpoints + idempotent processing
4. Stateful workflows (sagas, sessions): state in backing service; process stateless
5. WebSocket servers: external state ideal; sticky connections as trade-off

**Putting it together - 12-Factor Spring Boot service**

*Repo, Dockerfile, CI/CD, manifests all follow the factors*
- Maven build → container image with temurin base
- application.yml placeholders for env; secrets from Vault/CSI
- K8s Deployment + HPA for scaling
- Graceful shutdown config in Spring + K8s
- Testcontainers for integration tests
- JSON logs to stdout
- Flyway migrations + K8s Jobs for admin tasks

**Trade-offs and when to deviate**

*Why 12-Factor wins*
- Portability: any k8s/PaaS
- Scalability: horizontal built-in
- Maintainability: clear separation
- Observability: consistent stdout + env

*Costs*
- Lots of env vars painful; use ConfigMaps + Secrets
- Secrets in env visible to pod access; use Vault/CSI/RBAC
- Strict statelessness hurts caches; pragmatic: recomputable caches
- Fast startup vs Java bootstrap cost; AOT (Spring Native), SnapStart
- High-volume stdout can overrun pipes; sample/rate-limit

*Anti-patterns*
1. Config in code
2. Per-env repos
3. File-based logs (stdout is k8s-native)
4. JVM memory sessions
5. DB migrations outside release
6. Long sync startup (JPA warmup)
7. Health checks not checking dependencies

*When to deviate*
- Data services: StatefulSets, PVCs, backup strategy
- ML inference with large models: preload, readiness probe gate traffic
- Legacy: migrate incrementally, logs first
- Monoliths modernizing: externalize config + logs first

**Strategic take**
- 12-Factor is floor, not ceiling
- Following doesn't make you cloud-native; makes you deployable
- Modern adds observability, resilience, security, FinOps, progressive delivery
- Biggest benefit: onboarding speed; new service understood in 30 min; pipeline boilerplate
- Deviate for good reasons; deviating without knowing = snowflake services

**Interview angle**
- Don't recite all 12
- Connect principles to real code/infra
- Name factor, explain meaning, give Java/K8s example, note where it strains

**Bottom line**
- 12-Factor = minimum for cloud-native; modern layers on observability, resilience, security
- Stateless processes + env config + stdout logs = deployable anywhere
- Interview-wise: demonstrate application to real Spring Boot + K8s

beats.text: In 2011 Heroku engineers codified patterns they saw in reliably-deployable SaaS apps. The goal: apps that can be built once and deployed anywhere, scaled horizontally without architectural rework, and managed by simple orchestration (process-per-concern). It predates Kubernetes but reads like a design spec for Kubernetes. It's opinionated, language-agnostic, and pragmatic. Most modern cloud-native practices — containers, 12-factor is baked in — stateless services, env-based config, structured logging, graceful shutdown — trace back to these principles. When to use it: default for new web services, SaaS, microservices in cloud. Not all 12 factors apply equally to every system (databases themselves aren't 12-factor apps; they're backing services), but the principles guide design and ops.
